articles.title: Mississippi releases video showing fatal police shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley
articles.summary: The state attorney general’s office said this week its monthlong investigation found the officer’s use of force was appropriate, which an attorney for Wiley’s family has disputed.
articles.body: Mississippi released video Thursday showing the fatal shooting of a 1-year-old boy by a police officer whom state authorities have cleared of criminal wrongdoing. Kohen Wiley was killed in June when Senatobia Police Sgt. Hunter Foster fired his gun into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call. Kohen’s family says video of the fatal encounter shows the shooting was not justified. The Mississippi attorney general’s office said this week its monthlong investigation found that Foster’s use of force was appropriate. Foster’s attorney, Martin Zummach, has said his client had “no choice” but to shoot at the vehicle because it was going to hit him. Zummach confirmed to NBC News that he represents Foster and that Foster is the officer who fired his weapon. Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney representing Kohen’s family, said Foster was not in danger when he fired the shot that killed the 1-year-old. Crump said the video shows Foster fired the shot from the passenger side of the car. Kohen’s close relatives watched the video taken during the June 14 encounter in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia, about 40 miles south of Memphis, Tennessee. The video included imagery from the camera worn by the officer who shot and killed Kohen. Kohen would have celebrated his second birthday in early November, Crump said at a news conference Thursday. “The word ‘justified’ has haunted me,” Kohen’s maternal grandmother, Veronica Roberson, said at the news conference. “There’s no justification for that.” Roberson said that she found out from reading the news that the state had cleared the officer and that she also saw parts of the video that had been leaked online Wednesday. She called the lack of notice from the attorney general’s office and the leak of the video a “slap in the face” to her family. Zummach told NBC News by email that “the investigation and findings contradict the false narrative that has been spread the last 4 months.” He said that “there will still be those that find fault with the police combined with people who make their living issuing [divisive] opinions.” Video shows multiple angles of the fatal encounter The Mississippi Department of Public Safety on Thursday released video showing the shooting from multiple law enforcement officers’ body-worn cameras. Darkhorse Press, a Mississippi crime and community news outlet with a focus on law enforcement, posted some of the video on its website Wednesday. The organization’s founder, Therese Apel, is the department’s former communications director. The videos show two women, one holding a baby, running across the parking lot and entering a vehicle. Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop. The vehicle then accelerates forward as an officer steps toward it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side. The car continues to drive away before the video cuts out. Wiley’s family attorney says officers’ actions were reckless Crump said the officers’ response — running at the vehicle with guns drawn to apprehend alleged shoplifters — was excessive and reckless. Vellesiya Wiley previously denied that she and her friend stole diapers from the store, and they have not been charged, according to state and county court records. She has said she raised Kohen up to show officers that he was in the car. “Diapers are something a mother needs for a child. Diapers should never cost a baby their life,” Crump said. “This decision sends a message that a Black baby boy, his life, is not as valuable as the white diapers that he is wrapped in.” Zummach, Foster’s attorney, has said the video vindicates his client because he was in danger from the moving vehicle and had “no choice” but to fire his gun. “She came right at Hunter Foster and the other officer, and he had to shoot his weapon,” Zummach told The Associated Press. Wiley has disputed that her friend, who was driving, headed toward the officers. Crump said the video shows the fatal shot came from the side of the car, disputing that Foster was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family concluded the same. An image of the vehicle shows its shattered right front passenger window. The family’s legal team called for the federal government to investigate the shooting. Zummach said it was “strictly muscle memory” that prompted Foster to fire additional shots. “The one that went through the side glass that everybody’s going crazy about? That’s because she was moving so fast,” Zummach said. “Your brain can’t talk to your finger that fast to stop,” he added. Experts provide conflicting analysis Two use-of-force experts reviewed the video at the request of the AP but provided conflicting assessments, illustrating the complexity of the encounter. Charles “Joe” Key, a former Baltimore police lieutenant who frequently serves as an expert witness in police use-of-force cases, said that while it is a tragedy that a child was killed, the shooting was a split-second decision that Foster made as the vehicle drove toward him and another officer. He said the driver appeared to use the vehicle to commit assault with a deadly weapon. Wiley’s friend, who was driving, has not been charged. “The officer that fired the shots narrowly escaped being run over and appeared to touch the car as he was moving,” Key said. “The shooting was objectively reasonable.” But John P. Gross, an expert on police use of force against moving vehicles, said Foster used “really bad tactics.” “He should never have placed himself in a position where he could have been struck,” Gross said, adding that an accusation of shoplifting did not justify “use of deadly force on a fleeing suspect.”

articles.title: Venezuelans demand elections in first national protest in nearly two years
articles.summary: No date has been set to decide on a successor for Nicolas Maduro after the former president was captured by US forces.
articles.body:
Thousands of Venezuelans have taken to the streets in several cities to demand free elections and other political changes, in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years.

US President Donald Trump and acting President Delcy Rodriguez have said there would be elections, but no date has been set for a vote to decide on a successor for Nicolas Maduro, after the former Venezuelan president was captured by US forces in a military raid in January.

Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, who has been outside the country for nearly a year after living in hiding following a contested 2024 election, has said elections must take place by July 2027.

Her Vente Venezuela movement organised the protest, which took place in the capital Caracas and other cities, including Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal and Maracaibo.

“Seeing this makes me happy because I know change is possible,” said 18-year-old cosmetology student Leosmary Hernandez, as she gathered with hundreds of others in northern Maracay. “I’ve been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader and president, Maria Corina.”

“I went out to protest before, when things were much tougher, and I’m even less afraid today because I want my voice to be heard,” she added.

Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV).

PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture.

After the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV remained in power with the support of the White House.

US President Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president.

His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms.

Venezuela’s socialist movement, in power since 1999 under late President Hugo Chavez and then Maduro, has in the past deployed security forces against protesters, but government forces had minimal presence at protest sites on Thursday, and in many smaller cities demonstrators dispersed before dark.

The ruling Socialist Party called for its supporters to march from Caracas’ Plaza Venezuela, the same place the opposition planned to gather two hours later, to a location near the presidential palace to commemorate Breast Cancer Awareness Month.

Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, known for his close ties to the security services, was pictured on state television attending the march, while the opposition supporters moved their protest to a nearby location.

Talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government , aimed at remaking the top court and the electoral council ahead of eventual elections, held their latest session this month, but changes could take significant time.

The negotiations, backed by the US, do not include Machado’s political movement, though she has said she will not stand in the way of their progress.

Machado’s proxy Edmundo Gonzalez Urrutia claims to have won the 2024 election according to vote tallies by the opposition. But the government, which never released full counts, backed Maduro, as did the country’s legal and electoral institutions.

Machado has for years sought US support, aligning with hawks in the Trump team who argued that Maduro, through alleged links to drug gangs, represented a direct threat to US national security. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are facing drug and torture charges in the US. They have pleaded not guilty.

articles.title: Israeli military kills 2 in Hebron gun battle as tension soars in West Bank
articles.summary: Violence flaring as Israeli pogroms heighten tension across Palestinian territory.
articles.body:
The Israeli military said it has killed two Palestinians in a gun battle in the city of Hebron, in the occupied West Bank.

The military said it had killed two gunmen on Friday after they had attacked a reserve battalion near the illegal settlement of Telem. Israel’s ambulance service reported that at least six Israeli soldiers were injured, with two in critical condition.

The gun fight comes amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory, with Israeli settlers and soldiers engaging in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife, with aggression on the rise ahead of next week’s Israeli election.

Israeli sources report that the Palestinians were driving a car with an Israeli licence plate before shooting towards the soldiers near one of the many military checkpoints surrounding Hebron.

Witnesses in the area said the shooting lasted for 20 minutes, which complicated the process of evacuating the injured.

Images shared by the AFP news agency appear to show a man holding a handgun during the fight, and later lying on the floor surrounded by Israeli soldiers.

Reports from Hebron said that the Israeli military has arrested two Palestinians and locked down the city.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has cancelled a series of election-related engagements planned for Friday and is expected to speak later on the shootings.

Far-right national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir responded by calling for Israel to take full control over the occupied West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements, which are illegal.

“We have to act before it’s too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely,” he said in a statement.

Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim noted the precarious situation in the territory as settlers and Israeli security forces maintain pressure on the local population.

“This is coming at a time of great tension, not just before the Israeli elections, but there has been a ramp-up in attacks by settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank,” she said.

Israeli forces arrested 36 Palestinians during raids across the occupied West Bank on Thursday, as attacks on Palestinian farmers and their lands during the olive harvest season ramp up.

In Jenin governorate, Israeli forces raided towns and villages, arresting 10 Palestinians, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing data from the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.

The town of Tuqu in the Hebron governorate was also raided by soldiers, who arrested former prisoner Shorok al-Badan, along with five others from other parts of Hebron, according to Wafa.

The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said that Israeli forces also arrested 14 people in Khirbet Jawaya village of Masafer Yatta in Hebron, while Wafa reported that three other Palestinians were arrested across the Hebron governorate, citing a security source.

In Nablus and Jerusalem, three more Palestinians were arrested during Israeli raids in the village of Burin, the town of Awarta, and the Qalandiya refugee camp.

The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it documented 17 pogroms by Israeli forces and settlers on Thursday against Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest.

The incidents were recorded across occupied West Bank governorates, including Hebron, Qalqilya, Nablus, Ramallah and el-Bireh, Jenin and Salfit.

According to the Commission, the attacks included assaults on farmers, preventing them from reaching their land, theft of crops and agricultural equipment, damage and burning of olive trees, as well as arrests, threats at gunpoint and live fire.

The Commission says the pattern represents an escalation in attacks targeting the olive harvest and undermines Palestinians’ ability to access and cultivate their land and maintain their livelihoods.

Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers garnered international attention and condemnation. US Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained on Wednesday by the Israeli military with a warning while volunteering to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: Keeping Madhubala alive: The fight for Karachi’s captive elephants
articles.summary: Karachi’s last two African elephants remain in captivity. Their sisters are already dead. Will they survive?
articles.body:
At Karachi Zoo, Jude Allen sang, You Are My Sunshine, to an elephant he could not save.

Noor Jehan, the 17-year-old African elephant, was suffering. Allen recalls massaging her legs, nursing her bedsores and spending her final days beside her.

She died on April 22, 2023, surrounded by a few activists. Allen, 45, had held various corporate jobs while volunteering as an animal caregiver since an early age.

But Noor Jehan changed something in him, he said. “The day this wild African elephant rested her painful forehead on mine, and I hugged her for the first time – it all made sense,” he tells Al Jazeera.

Now three years later, Allen has turned the grief of Noor Jehan’s loss into care for one of her sisters, Madhubala, who also faces major health challenges. He is part of a growing campaign of Pakistani and international activists and doctors trying to save Madhubala, a victim, her carers say, not just of medical conditions, but also of a system that is simply unable to give animals in captivity the attention and facilities they need.

In 2009, four elephant calves captured in Tanzania were brought to Pakistan, allegedly through an animal trader.

Two of them, Noor Jehan and Madhubala, were kept at the Karachi Zoo, while their sisters Sonia and Malika were taken to Safari Park, a larger facility also in Pakistan’s largest city that has both a zoo and other viewing spaces for visitors to watch animals up close.

Then, in 2020, Pakistan was gripped by the story of Kaavan, an Asian elephant that had spent 35 years in the capital city of Islamabad, eight of them alone after his companion Saheli died. Four Paws, an international animal welfare organisation, helped move Kaavan to an animal sanctuary in Cambodia , where he now lives with other elephants.

That episode also shone a light on the Karachi sisters. At the time, Allen was helping a friend with another animal shelter, and came to know Four Paws was in town. He reached out to them, and they led him to Noor Jehan and Madhubala.

By 2021, Noor Jehan’s tusk was infected. She suffered from malnutrition and stress, too.

Allen and the other activists couldn’t save Noor Jehan, but the campaign had turned into a wider cry, demanding care and justice for captive animals in the urban jungle of Karachi, the coastal home to 20 million people.

One animal in particular became the focus of attention.

Named after an iconic Indian film actress from the mid-20th century, Madhubala was now the only African elephant at the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation-run zoo. She was alone, banging her head against the gate of her enclosure, Allen recalls. “She didn’t have a friend.”

Allen says she needed company – she wanted a friend.

Allen, along with Four Paws, helped prepare her for a move to Safari Park, so she could join her sister elephants, Sonia and Malika.

Four Paws assessed the elephants and found that they needed better diets, enrichment and medical treatment. The organisation recommended reuniting them.

The reunion came in November 2024. Four Paws documented the meeting between the siblings at Safari Park. Sonia approached Madhubala first. Malika followed. The three touched one another with their trunks and drank together.

But days later, on December 8, Sonia died, aged about 19, after collapsing in her enclosure. The park’s director initially described an apparent heart failure. Subsequent findings, reported by Four Paws, identified a severe bacterial infection associated with an advanced abscess on her foot.

Amir Khalil, a Four Paws wildlife vet involved in the elephants’ care, told The Associated Press at the time that “such infections don’t spread in one day”. Four Paws linked her death to prolonged unsuitable living conditions and malnutrition.

Meanwhile, Madhubala and Malika were both diagnosed with tuberculosis, although recent examinations reported by her veterinarian have indicated that Madhubala is no longer testing positive.

Now Madhubala, 22, is recovering after losing more than 200kg (440 pounds) and becoming too weak to get up safely after lying down.

Khalil, who has also rescued wild animals from multiple conflict zones, is one of the carers who has taken charge of Madhubala’s recovery. He told Al Jazeera that Madhubala had recovered 85 percent of her ability to walk, and was a good patient: “She really wants to follow the standard operation procedure and to adhere to the programme that I put in,” he says. That includes a “water massage for the leg with high-pressure water”.

He says the required medication needs to be administered properly, and treating all the wounds – and they were getting better when he left Pakistan a few days ago.

For Allen, the work began with Noor Jehan.

While she was unwell, he says he visited the zoo daily, checking that the elephants received their food on time and in the right quantities. During Noor Jehan’s final 10 days, he was a near-permanent presence there, assisting the medical team however he could.

Her death became the beginning of the “ I Am Noor Jehan ” movement, which Allen leads for animals in captivity. The Pakistan Animal Welfare Society (PAWS), with I Am Noor Jehan, held a memorial for Noor Jehan with artists, filmmakers, and other animal activists .

Then came Madhubala. Preparing her to enter a transport crate required patience. Allen describes an elephant who could be aggressive and difficult to approach. Four Paws specialists helped him understand her needs.

But delays to the relocation disrupted the training, he says. Madhubala became frustrated and bored. Allen tried football.

He entered her enclosure, an approach he acknowledges Four Paws did not endorse. The caretakers warned him too: Madhubala wasn’t in a playful mood.

But within 20 minutes, he says, Madhubala wanted the ball.

She picked it up with her trunk and hid it between her legs. Then she began teasing her caretakers who were trying to retrieve it, offering the ball before concealing it again.

The sessions helped him build a relationship with her, he says. Madhubala began responding eagerly to training again.

“Earning her trust was the most significant accomplishment.”

That trust is especially important to Allen because he believes that Noor Jehan, and then Sonia, could have been saved.

When Sonia was unwell, Allen says he had raised concerns with local authorities about her weight loss and a swelling beneath her body. He says those warnings were not adequately acted upon.

‘What was meant to be a sanctuary became a zoo’

The deaths of two of the four African elephants in Karachi raise questions about the resources, expertise and accountability behind keeping wild animals in public institutions, experts say.

Karachi Municipal Corporation has not procured any animals in the last 20 years, and the elephants were brought in long before his time, Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab said, speaking to Al Jazeera.

“I’ve always said that animal welfare should be paramount. Anyone who wants to come join hands, to look after the animal, we would be ready and willing to work with them,” he said.

He argued that his team at KMC had done whatever it could to look after Madhubala with Khalil and other doctors.

“Madhubala was being treated, and the good thing is, now, Dr Khalil is also saying things are moving in the right direction and we’ve got a third-party perspective endorsing whatever was being done,” Wahab said.

But Allen says Safari Park, where Madhubala was moved after Noor Jehan’s death, has been a disappointment. Allen says he helped develop Madhubala’s new enclosure there, working on landscaping and the procedures that caregivers needed to use to help her.

Moving her was supposed to change the conditions of her life. But at Safari Park, he says, people come right up to the elephants, feed them, and treat the facility like a zoo.

“What was meant to be a sanctuary became a zoo,” he says.

Javed Maher, the top wildlife official in the government of Sindh, the province containing Karachi, says elephants and wildlife need to be in their own habitat, and people caring for them need to have knowledge of animals.

Currently, the Safari Park enclosure for elephants is about 14 hectares, roughly 35 acres, according to Four Paws.

Mahar says he offered hundreds of acres in the rural country for these elephants so they can live freely.

“Karachi Zoo, along with the majority of the zoos of the country, is not capable,” he says.

But the elephants have remained at Safari Park.

Former Islamabad High Court Chief Justice Athar Minallah, in a landmark 2020 judgement, declared that animals had rights. It was that ruling that enabled the transfer of Kaavan to Cambodia, and two Himalayan bears to a sanctuary in Jordan. The zoo in Islamabad was closed, and all 878 animals kept there were released or relocated.

“That judgement remains the law, as no appeal was filed against it,” says Minallah speaking to Al Jazeera.

“Under this jurisprudence, Madhubala has the right to live in an environment where her social, behavioural, and psychological needs can be met,” he says.

To be sure, the challenges that officials like those at KMC and elsewhere face are also real.

Pakistan already faces profound human hardship. A United Nations account published in March says more than 60 percent of people in the country cannot afford a healthy diet.

Acquiring animals that require specialist care creates obligations lasting decades. Once confined, they depend on people for every meal, for movement, companionship and treatment.

But that, say analysts, is even more reason to “stop keeping them in our custody”, says Allen.

He last saw Madhubala on October 8, when he was assisting the Four Paws team. When there are lots of people, he says, she gets distracted easily.

But she can also get jealous for Allen’s attention. “She will literally throw rocks if she can at anyone talking to me,” he smiled.

articles.title: He left school after Class 3 following his father’s death; decades later, his poetry became the subject of PhD research and earned him the Padma Shri
articles.summary: Haldhar Nag did not spend years in classrooms studying literature, nor did he follow the conventional path to becoming a recognised poet.
articles.body: Haldhar Nag did not spend years in classrooms studying literature, nor did he follow the conventional path to becoming a recognised poet. He left school after Class 3, following his father’s death, and began working to support himself. Decades later, his poetry in Kosli, also known as Sambalpuri, became the subject of doctoral research, and he received one of India’s highest civilian honours, the Padma Shri, in 2016.Nag’s story is not simply about a man who achieved recognition despite limited formal education. It is also about how a literary voice rooted in the language, landscape and everyday experiences of western Odisha found its way into academic institutions.According to a March 2016 TOI report, five scholars were pursuing PhD research on his poetry at the time. Sambalpur University was also compiling his writings into a collection intended for academic use. The poet, who had studied only up to Class 3, had become a subject of serious literary study.From the classroom to a life of workNag was born on March 31, 1950, in Odisha’s Bargarh district. His father’s death when he was a child disrupted his education, and he could not continue beyond the third standard.Instead of pursuing further studies, he entered the workforce. Accounts of his early life describe him working as a dishwasher at a local sweet shop before moving to a school, where he worked as a cook for 16 years.The work brought him into contact with the everyday life of a school, but it did not mean he returned to formal education. He eventually borrowed Rs 1,000 from a banker to start a small shop selling stationery and eatables to students.These details matter because Nag’s later literary recognition did not emerge from an established academic career or a conventional publishing network. His journey began with work, financial constraints and a life outside the formal institutions that typically shape literary reputations.Yet he continued to develop his writing in Kosli, the language associated with western Odisha that became central to his identity as a poet.The poem that opened a new chapterNag’s first published poem, Dhodo Bargachh (The Old Banyan Tree), appeared in a local magazine in 1990. According to The Better India’s account, he had been writing folk stories in Kosli before publishing his first poem. The response encouraged him to send more work, and four additional poems were published.The banyan tree is a fitting starting point for understanding the literary world he would go on to build. Nag drew on the world around him, writing about nature, society, religion, mythology and social injustice. His work was not confined to personal observations; it also addressed oppression and the concerns of ordinary people.His own view of poetry, reported by The Better India in 2016, was direct: “In my view, poetry must have real-life connection and a message for the people.”That emphasis on lived experience helps explain why his writing attracted attention beyond its original audience. Nag was writing in a language familiar to the communities whose lives and traditions informed his work, rather than building his reputation through an English-language literary establishment.He became known as Lok Kabi Ratna, a recognition of his standing as a people’s poet.When his poetry became a subject for PhD researchThe contrast between Nag’s formal education and his academic recognition is striking. In 2016, The Better India reported that five scholars were pursuing doctoral research on his poetry. The same report said Sambalpur University was compiling his writings into a collection called Haldar Granthabali-2, intended to be used in the university’s syllabus.The significance was not merely that scholars were studying an individual poet. Nag’s work offered material for examining the language, folklore, cultural memory and social realities of western Odisha through literature created outside the conventional academic system.His writing also formed part of a wider effort to give Kosli-Sambalpuri literature greater recognition. A poet who had not progressed beyond primary school had produced work that researchers considered worthy of sustained academic examination.The number of five doctoral researchers is a figure reported in 2016; it should not be treated as a verified count of scholars currently researching him. Nevertheless, the report establishes that his poetry had already become a subject of doctoral study at that time.Recognition beyond his home regionNag received the Padma Shri in 2016 in recognition of his contribution to literature. His standing in the literary world was also acknowledged by the Sahitya Akademi, India’s national academy of letters.The academy’s official records list him as a joint recipient of the 2017 Bhasha Samman for Koshali-Sambalpuri. Its biographical note identifies him as a writer in the language, notes that his works have been translated into Odia, Hindi and English, and lists works including Mahasati Urmila, Tara Mandodari, Veer Sundar Sai and Rasia Kavi.These recognitions place Nag’s work within a larger literary conversation, one that extends beyond the region in which he began writing. His achievements also draw attention to the role of regional-language literature in preserving cultural traditions and recording experiences that may otherwise receive limited space in mainstream literary discussions.A different measure of educationNag’s story is sometimes framed as proof that formal education is unnecessary. That would be too simple a conclusion. His experience does not diminish the importance of schooling; rather, it shows that educational qualifications and literary ability are not the same thing.He missed out on years of formal education because of circumstances in childhood. He nevertheless developed a body of poetry that earned public recognition and attracted academic interest.The distinction matters. Nag did not need a doctorate of his own for his work to become worthy of doctoral research. His literary standing emerged from what he wrote, the language in which he wrote it and the cultural world his poetry recorded.His journey from leaving school after Class 3 to receiving the Padma Shri is remarkable in itself. But the more enduring part of the story is what happened to his words: they travelled from a local magazine into university study, from oral recitation into written collections, and from a regional literary tradition into wider recognition.Haldhar Nag’s life offers a reminder that a person’s education cannot be measured by certificates alone. Sometimes, the work of someone who had little opportunity to study formally becomes material through which others pursue the highest levels of academic learning.You use AI every day. articles.title: Grenade exercise sparked deadly fire at Canada military base, army says
articles.summary: High winds propelled the blaze across the army base in Wainwright, killing four soldiers and injuring dozens more.
articles.body:
A fire that killed four soldiers at a western Canadian military base was sparked by an exercise using live grenades, a military official said.

The deadly fire broke out on a grenade launcher range during military exercises on Saturday, with high winds propelling it across the base, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan, commander of the Canadian Forces Military Police Group, told reporters on Thursday.

“A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity,” she added, with the flames spreading to a training area at the Wainwright military base in Alberta.

Due to the blaze being in the “permanent danger area” of the range, firefighters were unable to directly combat it, Hanrahan added.

The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

The military base lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees.

About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.

Four soldiers died and 39 were injured, with 27 requiring hospitalisation. The incident was one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military.

The soldiers and reserve members were participating in exercises ahead of a planned deployment to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation.

The Wainwright base is one of the largest bases operated by the Canadian Armed Forces. It regularly hosts training exercises involving military personnel from NATO countries.

During the final months of World War II and for several months in 1946, the base was used as an internment centre for German prisoners of war.

articles.title: New £15m museum in Portsmouth charts history of Royal Marines
articles.summary: The new exhibition in Portsmouth Historic Dockyard features artefacts and immersive displays.
articles.body:
A new £15m museum charting more than 360 years of Royal Marines history is due to open in Portsmouth.

The Royal Marines Experience in the city's Historic Dockyard is the new home for the Royal Marines Museum, formerly based at Eastney before it closed in 2017.

Exhibits include all 10 Victoria Crosses awarded to the Royal Marines, while a Remembrance room allows families to reflect on those who lost their lives in service.

Matthew Sheldon, chief executive of Royal Navy Museums, said the new museum would be "the breathing heart of the Royal Marines community".

The former Royal Marines Museum closed due to the "irreversible deterioration" of its previous home at Eastney Barracks.

The new exhibition, in the 1840s Grade II-listed Boathouse 6 in Portsmouth Historic Dockyard, was previously scheduled to open in 2019 and has seen estimated costs rise from £10m to about £15m.

In May 2025, the project was awarded £4.4m of lottery funding after a previous £13m lottery bid was refused.

The previous attraction at Eastney received about 35,000 visitors a year. It is hoped being in the Portsmouth Historic Dockyard complex, which boasts 600,000 visitors a year, will boost numbers.

The new exhibition replaces the previous Action Stations Commando Experience at Boathouse 6.

Portsmouth Historic Dockyard, the base for the National Museum of the Royal Navy, is already home to several naval attractions, including HMS Victory, The Mary Rose and HMS Warrior.

The Royal Marines Experience combines storytelling with hands-on activities, multimedia displays and immersive technology to tell the history of the Marines within the armed forces.

Sheldon said the new museum would "connect this story to more people".

"We want to do something new and exciting. We want to blur the lines between history and experience - what those individual Royal Marines have done and still do for us now.

"I really think people are going to love it.

"This is a critical story. We want this to be the breathing heart of the Royal Marines community."

Uniforms, medals, kit and weapons dating back through the history of the Royal Marines are on display.

Among hundreds of historical and modern artefacts is a Green beret worn by Marine WGC "Molly" MacPherson during the Falklands conflict.

Visitors can also try physical challenges, including testing their strength and stamina in activities such as press‑ups, pull‑ups, rope climbs and rucksack lifts, each guided by a digital instructor.

Charlie Mallett, who served as the Marines' first female bugler in 1997 and whose father was also a Royal Marine, had donated her uniform and bugle to the old museum. They are among the artefacts in the new display.

Speaking at a preview event before the official opening, she said: "To see it today when I walked it, I did get very emotional."

Peter Helsby, who served in the Royal Marines between 1965 and 1974, said: "It's a modern-day museum, it's brought in the future of the Royal Marines as well as the past.

"I would recommend it - it's absolutely spot-on."

He described the Remembrance room as "a lovely touch".

Andy Williams, who was a Marine for 20 years until 1989, said the exhibition "brought back tremendous memories".

"All of us are involved in that story and that's what they've captured - the story behind the men."

articles.title: 28-day challenge: We know what keeps us healthy. Why don't we do it?
articles.summary: Four small habits, one a week, done together: how the 28-Day Challenge works In 2015, at 43, I sat in a cardiologist’s office with a healthy BMI and
articles.body: Four small habits, one a week, done together: how the 28-Day Challenge worksIn 2015, at 43, I sat in a cardiologist’s office with a healthy BMI and normal blood reports. Then he showed me my coronary calcium score. It put me in the 98th percentile for my age. I had coronary artery disease, and nothing in my routine check-ups had hinted at it.In the eleven years since, I have learned a great deal about blood markers, scans and the latest science. But the biggest lesson was the simplest. I already knew what to do. Eat more vegetables. Move after a meal. Get enough protein. Drink enough water. Our grandmothers told us all of this. Knowing was never the hard part. Doing it, every single day, was.Why we don’t do what we knowThree things keep most of us stuck.First, we commit to a habit only when we understand why it matters, yet health advice usually arrives as an order. The doctor says, “lose weight”, hands over a leaflet, and moves to the next patient.Second, most of us need someone to hold us accountable. Left alone, the walk gets skipped on the first busy evening.Third, working on your health is lonely. Everyone around you is ordering dessert.We built the 28-Day Challenge to tackle all three at once. But you can run the core of it yourself, with a notebook and a friend, starting tonight.The four habits, and why each one worksFor 28 days you add one small habit each week and keep the ones before it.Week 1: a salad before one meal. Day 1 is two slices of cucumber before lunch or dinner. That’s it. Fibre eaten first slows the rush of sugar into your blood, so the same meal produces a smaller spike. You build up from cucumber to a real bowl.Week 2: a short walk after that meal. Two minutes to begin with, then the length of one song, then a little more. Moving muscles pull glucose out of the bloodstream directly, which is why a post-meal stroll does more for blood sugar than the same walk at another hour.Week 3: more protein. A bowl of curd, a full bowl of dal, a handful of roasted chickpeas. Protein keeps you full for longer and, after 50, it is the main thing standing between you and muscle loss. There are easy ways to get enough even if you are vegetarian or vegan.Week 4: water, at set times through the day. Most people mistake mild thirst for hunger. Drinking on a schedule removes the guesswork, and we cover how to know what is too little and what is too much.By Day 28 the four sit together in one routine: salad first, then your meal, then a walk, with protein on the plate and water through the day.Why a group changes the oddsThe challenge runs in a single WhatsApp group. Every morning, one card tells you the day’s step. If you want, you post a photo of your plate or a line about your walk. Nobody is called out for a missed day. A perfect day isn’t needed; doing some version of it matters more.More than 500 people have been through the challenge so far. What we hear back is rarely about the number on the scale. Gitanjali, twelve months on, still walks after dinner every night and still cannot start lunch without her cucumber. She is not the exception. The most common message we get is surprise that something this small is still part of their day a year later.Something I did not expect: people who have never spoken start cheering each other on, just from seeing each other’s lunch. One member in her late sixties had known these habits for years. What was missing, in her words, was simple: “I didn’t have my tribe.”When a member has a question about their own health, a panel of doctors, dietitians and specialists answers it in the group, typically within a day. Members tell us this is where they learn the most: answers specific to them, from people who know.What it is notThere is no shortage of diets, apps, and influencers. This is deliberately small. One habit a week. No diet to follow and no food to give up. It is also deliberately modest. It is not here to replace your doctor; your doctor is still your doctor. If you have a medical condition, follow their advice first.Each week opens with a one-hour call on the science behind that week’s habit and simple ways to fit it into a real life. After Day 28, most people stay on in our free community, The Longevity Circle. That community exists because a few people from our first round refused to leave the WhatsApp group.Living a healthy life should not feel like a sacrifice. It should be fun. Start with two slices of cucumber, and see where 28 days take you.The next challenge starts Monday, November 16, with a live kick-off call on Sunday, November 15. It costs ₹999 in India and $49 outside India; details at try28.com.(Nickhil Jakatdar, PhD, is the CEO of GenePath Diagnostics and the co-founder and chairman of PreventiveHealth.ai, which runs The Longevity Circle and the 28-Day Challenge.)Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: 'Just a carpet of dead birds' - first England farmer hit by bird flu this season
articles.summary: The first farmer in England hit by bird flu this season tells of the "emotional roller coaster" of losing 32,000 hens.
articles.body:
A farmer hit by England's first outbreak of avian flu this season has said the loss of 32,000 egg-laying birds is likely to cost her business more than £100,000.

Catherine Armstrong, who has a free-range farm near Belford, Northumberland, told the BBC of the "shock" of her worst fears coming true when she found "a carpet of dead birds" in her barns this week.

The outbreak's source is not yet known but the virus is thought to have been brought onto the site, which has strict biosecurity measures, by wild birds. The farm's remaining poultry were culled.

The Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) has put control measures in place to contain the outbreak but warned cases were likely to rise.

So far, there has been one other case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in the UK , on the Isle of Lewis, Scotland.

Armstrong said her birds, which normally produce 28,500 eggs a day, which are then supplied to a range of UK supermarkets, began to die a week ago.

"At this age of the flock, you would tend to see the odd death but on the Friday my lady who works in the shed messaged me at night to say that 39 had died," she explained.

During the weekend, the virus spread rapidly, with more than 1,000 birds dead by Sunday night.

The APHA was contacted and a vet came out to carry out tests but Armstrong said she knew it would be bird flu: "In my heart of hearts, when you are shovelling dead birds out of a shed, you feel... well, I didn't need the results. I knew what the results would be."

By Tuesday, the virus had been confirmed, with thousands of birds dead. Within two days, all the remaining birds had been culled to control the virus' spread.

"All your worst fears, I suppose, are realised then. It is an emotional roller coaster. I mean, for instance, on the Sunday, I just felt numb. On the Monday, just a bit like 'Why me?'. Angry, cross, upset.

"On the Tuesday, it's a bit matter of fact. It's like, 'Right, we've got to do this. I've got to do that'. And on Wednesday, I was just desperately sad.

"Normally, you'd open up a hen shed door and there'd be 16,000 birds looking at you but to see them all lying dead, just a carpet of dead birds, is quite shocking.

"As a poultry keeper, it's a horrible shock."

Armstrong praised the APHA staff for their work and the wider industry for its support.

She said despite the high cost of the outbreak - which she estimated would be more than £100,000 - she was "not going to sit back and let it beat us".

Gary Ford, of the British Free Range Egg Producers' Association (Bfrepa), said the farm had high standards of biosecurity but "sadly, as was the case here, that does not always prevent infection as free-range hens come into regular contact with wild birds, which spread this dreadful disease".

He added the association would be calling on the government to bring in a regional housing order to protect "those poultry farms close to coastal areas and known flight paths of migratory wild birds".

Meanwhile, farmers are still waiting for the results of a recent government trial of a bird flu vaccine in turkeys .

A spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said that, while the trial concluded in August, results would not be available until the end of the year and vaccination would not be an option for this bird flu season.

Meanwhile, an APHA spokesperson said it expected colder temperatures and the arrival of migratory birds "to see a rise in infection cases, which is why it is so important that bird keepers have robust biosecurity measures in place to limit the spread of this devastating disease".

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the risk to the general public's health posed by avian influenza remained very low while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said it posed a very low food safety risk, with properly cooked poultry and poultry products, including eggs, safe to eat.

articles.title: Adults with ADHD left struggling to access treatment in NI
articles.summary: Northern Ireland is the only part of the UK without a formally commissioned, publicly-funded adult service for ADHD.
articles.body:
Adults with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are demanding urgent action over a lack of funded services in Northern Ireland, with some revealing they pay thousands of pounds a year for private treatment.

Northern Ireland doesn't have a formally commissioned, publicly funded adult ADHD pathway like in other parts of the UK.

One woman has described the situation as "wildly unfair and inhumane", saying she and her husband spend about £4,000 a year on private treatment and care.

The Department of Health acknowledges increasing demand but said decisions must be taken in the context of overall affordability.

'It's a tonne of money that most people don't have'

Rebecca Bryson owns three businesses, which helps to cover the cost of her ADHD treatment and follow up care.

Her husband, Colum Coyle, also has ADHD, and both pay for regular private psychiatric reviews, prescriptions and medication. Their combined costs of staying on treatment are about £4,000 a year.

"It's a tonne of money that most people don't have, and I'm in a position where we do have it because I work multiple jobs," she said.

She said the situation felt "wildly unfair and kind of inhumane".

"If I had another medical condition like cancer or a broken bone, and I asked for medical treatment, they wouldn't turn me away."

Bryson said there needed to be a clear route to diagnosis for adults with ADHD in Northern Ireland.

"You can get a diagnosis as a child, but once you turn 18, you're on your own. It's bananas."

Northern Ireland : Remains without a formally-commissioned ADHD service. Trusts manage referrals within existing resources, leading to long waiting lists.

England : A legal right to choose exists in areas within England. If a local wait is long, a GP can refer a patient to another NHS-approved provider.

Scotland: There is no single commissioned service for ADHD, as local statutory partners have responsibility for planning, designing and delivering services to meet the neurodevelopmental support needs locally, including services commissioned from the third sector where appropriate.

Wales : ADHD services are commissioned locally by health boards. The Welsh government is working through its Neurodiverse Improvement Programme to increase capacity, improve assessment pathways and reduce long waiting lists.

Dr Allen McCullough has worked as a GP for 35 years. He said he understands the difficulties with those seeking ADHD diagnoses and it has become an "evolving picture".

"I can refer to an adult ADHD service within my local area, but that's in the full knowledge that there isn't anybody there to receive it," he said.

McCullough says some GPs have concerns issuing medication for those looking shared-care arrangements, where a consultant and GP collaborate to manage and prescribe specialist medications.

"Some of these patients are attending privately, and we don't get any notification of who they're seeing or the qualification of the person who's doing the diagnosis. So, I'm not saying it isn't a stand over diagnosis, but if we're not getting the information, we're definitely not going to get involved or cannot get involved.

"When you prescribe it, you're responsible."

Jordan Young, 28, said he struggled to get access to ADHD services, which typically include assessments, medication and follow-ups.

"I tried so many different places. I was basically told that the doors were closed, they weren't taking anyone else on," he said.

"If it wasn't for my granny, I wouldn't have gone over and gone private to be honest. She put me through her private health insurance."

Young said more needed to be done to improve access to ADHD services in Northern Ireland.

"I want to see where the health minister actually comes to some sort of agreement that he will put a budget [in] for people with ADHD or people that looking to be diagnosed with ADHD and treat it like it is a serious matter."

Alliance MLA Peter McReynolds said adults with ADHD had been "completely forgotten about" by the Department of Health.

He said he had been pushing for a commissioned service since 2024 and had met three health ministers, who he said had taken a similar approach.

"I think we should be a hell of a lot further [on] in terms of commissioning that service because it would be transformative for the people of Northern Ireland and it would save us money in the longer term as well."

A Department of Health spokesperson said health trusts "manage referrals within existing resources and demand continues to exceed available capacity, resulting in long waiting times which has led to people seeking a private diagnosis".

"Significant work has been undertaken to better understand the level of need for ADHD services," he said.

"Any future commissioning decisions must be taken in the context of overall affordability, at a time when we face significant funding constraints across health and social care."

articles.title: Meet the Stoke-on-Trent pensioners finding new ways to cut costs
articles.summary: Errol McGuiness says he has changed his daily routine to cope with higher household bills.
articles.body:
As evenings grow colder and household budgets come under renewed pressure, 79-year-old grandad Errol McGuiness has developed a routine to keep costs down.

The pensioner collects rainwater, spends much of his time in a single room and piles on extra layers rather than turning up the heating.

"I keep lots of clothes on, but don't tell my daughter," he said.

His most striking money-saving measure comes when night falls.

"You don't need a light on to watch telly. You don't need a light on when you go to bed. You know the way to the toilet and the kitchen, so you don't need a light on."

Errol admits he has a health condition and says his daughter regularly reminds him to switch the heating on.

But he is far from alone in trying to cut household costs.

New figures published this week showed inflation rose to 3.5% in September, its highest level for almost a year, while higher fuel prices have pushed up living costs for many households.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised measures aimed at easing pressure on household finances, including removing standing charges from gas bills.

Four years into the cost-of-living crisis, almost two-thirds of low-income families say they struggle to afford essentials such as food, heating and clothing, according to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Almost half said they had skipped meals or reduced portion sizes to save money.

Among them is 83-year-old widower Bryan, who says he now lives largely in a single room to keep bills down.

"I put a cardigan on and whatever it is you put on to keep yourself warm, shut the door, put the fan heater on to warm the house up," he said.

"When you see the price keep going up, I think,' well, I'm sitting in one room'."

At Affordable Foods in Blurton, Stoke-on-Trent, centre manager Melissa Baydilly says stories like Errol's and Bryan's are becoming increasingly common.

The organisation runs a food bank, social supermarket and outreach service helping people with debt, benefits and employment issues.

"Every supermarket you go into, everything's gone up," she said.

"There isn't a place where you would go now and not say there's at least a 25% to 30% hike on prices."

She believes pensioners are among those feeling the strain most acutely.

"I don't believe, in this day and age, our seniors of the city should go to the supermarket, look at the fruit and veg and think, 'I can't have apples and oranges this week, I've got to pick'.

"Should they be doing that in their 60s and 70s, when they've worked all their life?"

articles.title: Northampton composer Malcolm Arnold 'should be better known'
articles.summary: The renowned cellist says the annual music festival is "keeping Sir Malcolm's name alive".
articles.body:
The renowned cellist Julian Lloyd Webber says the Northampton composer Malcolm Arnold should be "much better known than he is".

Lloyd Webber will launch the 21st Malcolm Arnold Festival in the Oscar-winning composer's hometown on Saturday.

Sir Malcolm, who died in Norwich in 2006 aged 84 , won an Academy Award for his score of the 1957 film The Bridge on the River Kwai, which tells a story of British prisoners of war captured by the Japanese during World War Two.

Lloyd Webber, who worked with Arnold, said: "He was a character, and an extraordinary man."

The festival first took place in 2006 to celebrate Sir Malcolm's 85th birthday, but he died two weeks before it began.

This year there will be a world premiere performance of the composer's unfinished Violin Concerto, orchestrated from his detailed sketches.

Lloyd Webber's wife, Jiaxin Cheng Lloyd Webber, herself an acclaimed cellist, will perform the work written by Sir Malcolm for her husband, which he will introduce.

Julian Lloyd Webber, the brother of Lord Andrew Lloyd Webber, retired in 2014 due to a neck injury, which left him unable to play.

He said: "Arnold was a really wonderful composer, he should be much better known than he is.

"He wasn't the easiest person to work with but he wrote wonderful music."

Lloyd Webber said Sir Malcolm "had his problems with the music establishment" because his melodic style was not well received at the time.

But he described him as a "genius" at film music, having written 132 scores including Whistle Down the Wind and Hobson's Choice, and said he was a "prolific" composer.

"Everyone wanted him, there was a time when all the virtuosos of the time wanted him to write something for their instrument," he said.

He said the festival was "keeping Malcolm's name alive and it's introducing people to his beautiful music and they'll be a lot richer for hearing it".

Festival organiser Paul Harris said Malcolm Arnold "wrote music for people to play to other people".

He told Bernie Keith on BBC Radio Northampton that he always believed the festival would be well supported in Sir Malcolm's hometown.

Harris said: "There is something about Malcolm, his life, the fact he was a Northampton man, his family were in shoes, there is something very personal about [the festival].

"The music, it speaks to people, and people like to be communicated with, it's what draws us in and he knew how to do it."

articles.title: In 2021, more than 9 inches of rain poured over a Mississippi home; State Farm refused to pay about $16,000 for a full roof replacement, but a 2025 appeals court reversed the dismissal and sent the case back
articles.summary: In a significant legal battle, a Mississippi couple's claim for a new roof after a devastating storm was initially denied by State Farm, but an appeals court reverses the dismissal and allows the case to proceed, highlighting important insurance policy distinctions.
articles.body: Few insurance disputes are as familiar as the one that follows a heavy downpour. When rain gets into a house, the roof is blamed, but the homeowner and the insurer often cannot agree on the cause. Who pays depends on whether the roof was already in poor condition or was damaged by the storm. Behind that sits a bigger question: who must prove what.That question ended up in federal court after a storm passed through Greenwood, Mississippi, in June 2021. Rain streamed into their house, and Mark and Margie Barger asked State Farm to pay for a brand new roof. The insurer disputed about $16,000 of the claim, and a lower court agreed. But in March 2025, the Fifth Circuit, the US federal appeals court covering Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas, overturned the ruling on the burden of proof, vacated the dismissal and sent the case back to the lower court.The storm and the roofIt was a bad storm. Almost 8 inches of rain fell on June 10 alone, and the storm total came to about 9.25 inches, or roughly 23.5 cm, according to the Fifth Circuit’s opinion. Water poured through the roof and ceilings of the Bargers’ single-storey house in at least seven places, and all three bedrooms, the dining and living rooms, a hallway and the foyer were affected.The couple said their eleven-year-old roof had never leaked before that night and kept leaking afterwards. The insurer paid for the interior damage and the couple’s belongings but would not pay for a new roof. Its position was that the only covered roof damage came from nine wind-damaged shingles and a small patch of roofing membrane. In plain terms, the insurer accepted that the storm had done some harm, just not enough to justify a new roof. The Bargers paid for a replacement themselves in March 2022 and sued for breach of contract two months later. The amount still in dispute was $16,023.79, plus an extra $3,120 to $5,000 in higher material costs.Who must prove whatThe district court granted summary judgment to State Farm, resolving the dispute without trial. The rationale was that the policy covered wind and hail, but not wear, decay or latent faults, and that the Bargers had not shown evidence indicating a covered event caused the additional damage. It also found that the only expert testimony as to cause pointed to faults in the construction.The problem, the appeals judges found, was that the district court had applied the wrong burden of proof. It had relied on the policy wording for personal property, which lists specific risks such as windstorm or hail, instead of the wording for the dwelling itself. Dwelling coverage is different. Insurers call this all-risk protection, which covers accidental direct physical loss unless an exception applies.That disparity changes the burden of proof under Mississippi law, the state Supreme Court said in a 2009 case, Corban v. USAA. Simply put, the question is who has the burden of proof to establish why the water got in. With all-risk coverage, the homeowner only has to prove that a physical loss occurred. After that, it is up to the insurer to prove that an exclusion such as wear and tear accounts for it. With a named-perils policy, the burden shifts and it is the policyholder who must prove that the harm was caused by a covered hazard. The trial court misstated the test, and thereby imposed an additional and more onerous duty on the Bargers.State Farm contended that the mistake was a clerical error that didn’t matter. The appeals court wasn’t persuaded and wrote that water had spilt into seven separate portions of the property, enough to create a genuine issue of material fact as to whether the roof system sustained accidental physical loss in the storm.What happens nextThe appeals court did not order any payment to the Bargers. In particular, it declined to opine on whether either side had met its burden on the policy exclusions, such as wear and tear or structural faults, leaving that to the district court when the case returns to it. The insurer may still argue the damage was caused by the way the roof was built or by wear. The difference now is that the insurer must prove an exclusion applies.Policyholders who think a claim has been mishandled can contact their state regulator. The Mississippi Insurance Department accepts complaints online and sends a copy to the insurer. It asks for supporting paperwork such as a denial letter and a copy of the policy within two working days and says it cannot aid anyone already represented by a lawyer or who needs legal guidance.Keeping dated photos of leaks, storm data, and proof of the roof’s prior condition gives a claim something concrete to rest on, regardless of who bears the burden. The insurer’s argument that only a tiny portion of the roof was storm damaged has yet to be tested at trial. The ruling was not published, so it is not binding on other courts.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, Wyoming’s Supreme Court rejected a landowner’s bid for a private road across his neighbour’s property; he wanted to reach a riverside meadow below a 60-foot drop
articles.summary: In its 2025 ruling, Wyoming's Supreme Court upheld a decision denying a landowner access to a riverside meadow by rejecting his request for a private road through a neighbor's property. The court clarified legal standards for access rights and easements in land disputes.
articles.body: Roads, easements, and the goodwill of neighbours are the main sources of access in most places. Until someone wants to build, farm, or just walk to a beloved location, the gaps in that arrangement usually go unnoticed. When a dispute arises, courts must determine whether the need is real or merely a question of preference.Wyoming’s top court answered that question in 2025. On May 23, the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled against Samuel Tilden, who wanted a private road across his neighbour Linda Jackson’s land to reach a level meadow beside the South Fork of the Shoshone River, below a hillside with a 60-foot drop, or about 18 metres. The judges upheld two earlier Park County district court rulings. They said his land was not landlocked because a county road already ran through it, and that a steep slope on his own property was not the kind of problem the statute is meant to remedy.The land and the dropTilden bought the property in 1996 and sold 23 acres, roughly 9 hectares, to Jackson and her late husband in 2010, keeping the area around it. He lived on a portion of what he retained until 2021, when he sold his house and the acreage to the west and south of Jackson’s property. He kept a final lot of 2.64 acres to the north. A county road ran straight through it on the steep hillside. Below it lay the river meadow, and the only way down was a very steep game trail that no car or ATV could use.Tilden testified that he retained the land so he could reach a favourite fishing spot. Before he divided up the property, he and his family had walked across what became Jackson’s land via a two-track road to the lower terrain to fish, skate on the ice, ride horses or walk the dogs. After the 2021 sale, he rented a cabin from Jackson and put a corral on the meadow, relocated six horses there and still used the same road to feed them.But January 2022 changed everything. Tilden planned to build a new cottage on the lower ground, so he moved out of the cabin he had been renting from Jackson. He offered to buy Jackson’s 23 acres, but she declined and told him she didn’t want him crossing her land anymore. He sued in June 2022, seeking the implied easement or a private road under Wyoming law.Why the private road failedWyoming’s constitution bars the taking of private land for private use without the owner’s consent, with one exception for private ways of necessity. A state law turns that exception into a process, but the applicant has to show the road is truly needed. In practice that means proving the land is landlocked, with no legally enforceable route to a public road, or that the existing route is so inconvenient that the difference amounts to necessity.Tilden could not pass the test. He admitted that the county road passed across his land and that he had a legal interest in the same, and he did not contend that the road in itself was very inconvenient. The actual grievance was that a natural barrier on his own property separated him from the lower level. That, the court said, was not the sort of necessity the law contemplates. The statute is meant to prevent landlocking, it stated, not to make a property easier to use or more valuable to sell.The easement claimAn implied easement can arise when one owner splits a property and, before the split, used a route across one part to serve the other. Three things must be shown. The land was once under common ownership and was later divided, the earlier use was apparent, obvious and continuous, and the route is necessary and beneficial to the land that relied on it.The trial judge looked at aerial images taken shortly after the separation and found no obvious trail from the county road over Jackson’s land to the meadow. The photos showed only a short loop around the well pump. A neighbour testified that he had never seen a way to the meadow, only a short track round the pump, and Jackson said she had assumed the track was for the well. The Supreme Court noted that it was more than ten years after the division of the property that Tilden first thought of building a cottage and corral below the drop. He also had not proved that he could not build on the 2.64 acres or continue using the game trail for fishing and other family activities.What landowners can take from itThe decision is a reminder that access rights are best settled on paper at the moment land is divided. Anyone who sells part of a property while keeping another should work out how they will reach what remains and secure an easement in the sale documents, rather than relying on years of informal use. Without a written right, a neighbour’s goodwill can end, as it did here.For owners whose land really has no legal way out, Wyoming does offer a remedy. The constitutional exception for private ways of necessity and the state’s private road law have been explained by the Wyoming Supreme Court in earlier cases, including a 2007 ruling that traces the law back to 1895 and says damages are measured by comparing a property’s value before and after the road. That ruling notes that the original statute was amended in 2000, and the current procedure is set out in Wyoming Statute § 24-9-101. The constitutional wording it quotes also requires just compensation for any such taking.The other side of the coin is the Tilden case. A cliff, a game trail and a pleasant memory of fishing were not enough to compel a neighbour to give up a piece of her land. The court made it plain that the law protects those whose property would otherwise be useless and that seeking a better route to part of one’s own land is something else. Owners who want to develop in hard-to-reach corners of their property should check their access before they buy and ask for it in writing before they sell.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Australian chicken farmer found a way to turn 35,000 tonnes of poultry waste into electricity, fertiliser and natural food dye; a larger plant could power 1,200 homes
articles.summary: An Australian poultry farmer is developing a system that could turn thousands of tonnes of chicken waste into electricity, fertiliser and natural food
articles.body: An Australian poultry farmer is developing a system that could turn thousands of tonnes of chicken waste into electricity, fertiliser and natural food colouring, creating multiple products from a material that is commonly used as agricultural manure. Chris Freney, who operates a poultry farm in Toongabbie, in Victoria's Gippsland region, has been exploring ways to extract energy and recover nutrients from poultry litter. His proposed larger facility is designed to process 35,000 tonnes of litter annually and generate enough electricity to meet the estimated needs of around 1,200 homes. The project combines anaerobic digestion, a process that produces biogas from organic material, with nutrient recovery and the cultivation of spirulina, an algae used to produce natural blue pigments.How an Australian farmer plans to turn chicken waste into electricityFreney's approach centres on anaerobic digestion, in which microorganisms break down organic material in an oxygen-free environment, producing biogas and a nutrient-rich residue called digestate. Poultry litter contains more than manure: it also includes bedding materials such as wood shavings or sawdust, along with feathers and spilled feed.During digestion, organic matter produces biogas containing methane, which can be captured and burned in an engine connected to an electricity generator. The resulting power could supply the poultry operation, while surplus electricity could be exported to the grid.The process also leaves behind liquid and solid materials containing nutrients that can be recovered for agricultural use. Instead of treating the litter solely as waste or applying it directly to land, the system aims to extract energy and recover useful components before putting the remaining material to work.A larger plant could process 35,000 tonnes annuallyFreney's farm reportedly produces about 10,000 tonnes of poultry litter each year. To supply the proposed larger facility, he would need to source additional material from other poultry farms, taking the planned annual input to 35,000 tonnes.Reports have put the proposed electricity-generation capacity at approximately 8 to 8.5 megawatts, with the output described as sufficient to power around 1,200 homes. The household figure is an estimate rather than a measurement of electricity already delivered to homes.Freney has said that the facility could use a substantial share of its electricity on the farm and sell the remainder. He has also discussed supplying power during evening peak-demand hours, when solar generation is unavailable.The project has an environmental development licence from the Environment Protection Authority Victoria. However, the published licence describes a configuration designed to process 15,000 tonnes of organic waste annually, with a 1.1-megawatt combined heat and power unit. These specifications differ from the larger capacity reported for the proposed expansion.The project’s final capacity, construction progress and commissioning status are therefore important to understanding how the larger proposal relates to the licensed facility.The unusual plan to make natural blue food colouringOne of the project's distinctive features is its proposed production of natural blue food colouring from spirulina, a blue-green microalga. Rather than turning chicken manure directly into a food ingredient, the process uses nutrients recovered from the waste to support algae cultivation.Spirulina can produce blue pigments, including phycocyanin, which is used as a natural colourant in certain food products. The algae must be harvested and processed to extract the pigment, with the resulting ingredient meeting applicable food-safety and quality requirements.This creates a potential additional revenue stream alongside electricity and fertiliser. It also illustrates how nutrient recovery can connect agricultural waste management with a separate industry.The commercial viability of this part of the project will depend on factors such as algae yields, processing costs, product quality and demand from food manufacturers.Fertiliser offers another use for the wasteThe residue left after anaerobic digestion contains nutrients that may be used to produce fertiliser. Recovering these nutrients can help return useful material to agriculture and reduce the amount of untreated waste requiring management.The environmental benefits depend on how the digestate is handled and applied. Appropriate storage, nutrient management and application rates remain important because excess nutrients can enter waterways through runoff. Anaerobic digestion also requires energy and can produce greenhouse gas emissions if methane escapes from the system.The approach is therefore best understood as a waste-recovery model that seeks to extract several useful products from poultry litter, rather than as a process that eliminates every environmental impact.Why the project matters for Australian farmingElectricity is a significant operating expense for poultry farms, where heating, ventilation and other equipment must run to maintain suitable conditions for birds. Freney has previously invested in solar panels on his eight poultry sheds, reporting annual savings of about A$40,000 on energy bills.A biogas system could complement solar power by generating electricity from stored organic material, including during periods when sunlight is unavailable. Selling surplus power and recovering nutrients could provide additional sources of income.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Australian TV reporter recalls ‘terrifying’ rescue of man from sinking car
articles.summary: An Australian television reporter who rescued a man from a car as it was engulfed by floodwaters said Friday that it was terrifying to watch someone almost drown but added that “there are few better feelings” than saving a person’s life.
articles.body: SYDNEY — An Australian television reporter who rescued a man from a car as it was engulfed by floodwaters said Friday that it was terrifying to watch someone almost drown but added that “there are few better feelings” than saving a person’s life. Will Murray, a journalist with public broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, was reporting on flooding north of the city of Brisbane in Queensland state on Thursday, when a man drove a four-wheel drive through floodwater. It then stalled and started to sink. “It was terrifying. Like, the thought of watching someone drown was just, you know, I can see why people would sort of freeze up, because it is just horrifying to watch someone in distress like that,” Murray told Reuters. Murray and bystander Daniel Hainey swam out to the car and pulled the driver from the vehicle, moments before it was completely submerged. Murray did not get the survivor’s name or number, but said he hoped the man was doing well. “You know, we had a big old hug after we got him out, and that was just one of the best moments of my life, I have to say, just the relief of seeing him safe and well. That was enough for me,” Murray said. Emergency services in southeast Queensland responded to hundreds of distress calls on Thursday and Friday after more than 7.9 inches of rain caused flash flooding that closed roads and schools.
